title: Magnetic Moment, Interstitial, Alloys, Complexes, IP & Density
subtitle: Magnetic Moment, Interstitials, 7 Alloys, Complexes, Ionization Enthalpy & Density

magnetic.heading: Magnetic Properties
magnetic.p1: Most transition metals and their compounds exhibit paramagnetism (attracted to magnetic fields).
magnetic.p2: Magnetic behaviour depends on the number of unpaired electrons. Substances with unpaired electrons are paramagnetic. Most elements from d¹ to d⁹ are paramagnetic.
magnetic.p3: Substances where all electrons are paired, such as d⁰ and d¹⁰ ions, are diamagnetic (repelled by magnetic fields).
magnetic.formulaLegend: Spin-only magnetic moment formula: μ = √(n(n+2)) Bohr Magnetons (B.M.), where n = number of unpaired electrons.

interstitial.heading: Interstitial Compounds
interstitial.p1: Small interstitial spaces (voids) exist inside the crystal lattices of transition metals. When small non-metal atoms such as Hydrogen, Boron, Carbon, or Nitrogen (H, B, C, N) occupy these spaces, the resulting substances are called interstitial compounds.
interstitial.p2: These compounds are extremely hard, possess very high melting and boiling points, retain metallic electrical conductivity, and are chemically relatively inert. Their ductility and malleability are lower than pure metals.
interstitial.examples: Examples: Steel, cast iron, and TiC (Titanium carbide).

alloys.heading: Alloys
alloys.p1: Due to similar atomic sizes (within 15%), transition metal atoms can readily substitute for one another in crystal lattices to form alloys when melted together.
alloys.p2: Alloys are far more utilitarian than pure metals: much harder, higher melting points, and highly resistant to corrosion/rusting.

complexes.heading: Coordination Complexes
complexes.p1: Transition metals readily form complex compounds with ligands via coordinate covalent bonds. The driving factors are small cation size, high charge density, and availability of vacant d, s, and p orbitals to accept electron pairs.
complexes.p2: These coordination complexes are exceptionally stable and retain their distinct identity even in aqueous solution.

ip.heading: Ionization Enthalpy
ip.p1: The minimum energy required to remove the outermost electron from an isolated gaseous atom.
ip.p2: Ionization enthalpies of transition elements are higher than s-block metals but lower than p-block non-metals.
ip.p3: Along a transition series, increasing nuclear charge is opposed and balanced by increasing shielding from (n-1)d electrons, causing ionization enthalpy to increase very slowly and irregularly.
ip.order: Order of IP for 3d series: Sc < Ti > V < Cr < Mn < Fe > Co > Ni < Cu < Zn

density.heading: Density Trends
density.p1: Density increases along the series due to decrease in metallic radius combined with increase in atomic mass. A steady increase is seen from Ti to Cu.
density.p2: In the entire d-block, Osmium (Os) and Iridium (Ir) have the highest densities (~22.6 g/cm³), while Copper has the highest in the 3d series.
density.order: 3d Density order: Sc < Ti < V < Cr < Mn < Fe < Co < Ni < Cu > Zn (Increases from Ti to Cu, drops at Zn)
density.lanthanoidEffect: Due to Lanthanoid Contraction, density rises dramatically down the group: Ti < Zr <<< Hf; Cu < Ag <<< Au.
